Smoke is seen billowing out of the ground and first floor of the Taj Hotel in south Mumbai during security personnel’s “Operation Cyclone” following the 26/11 terror attacks in 2008. File photo | Photo Credit: PTI
On November 26, 2008, 10 Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorists from Pakistan arrived by sea and killed 166 people, including 18 security personnel, besides injuring more than 300 others during a 60-hour siege of Mumbai. The terrorists targeted several high-profile locations, including the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi Trident, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus and Nariman House.
But the city has been rattled by other attacks too, including the horrific 1993 Mumbai blasts. As Mumbai marks the anniversary of the 26/11 attacks, here is a look at some of the other major terror attacks that have struck the city over the years.
On March 12, 1993, 13 coordinated serial blasts ripped through Mumbai’s commercial and social hubs, killing 257 people and injuring more than 700. The city was still recovering from the communal riots of December 1992 and January 1993 that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid on December 6, 1992, when the bombs exploded at regular intervals across Mumbai.
The attacks, the first of their kind in India, are believed to have been carried out in retaliation for the post-Babri Masjid demolition riots in Mumbai.
A month later, the Mumbai Police arrested Hindi film actor Sanjay Dutt for possessing an AK-56 rifle that was believed to be part of the arms consignment linked to the attacks. Although investigators could not establish his involvement in the conspiracy, his possession of the weapon and subsequent attempt to destroy it drew scrutiny. He was sentenced to six years in prison for illegally possessing automatic weapons linked to the consignment used in the attacks.
The alleged masterminds of the blasts, gangsters Tiger Memon and Dawood Ibrahim, remain absconding.
On March 13, 2003, a powerful explosion tore through the first-class compartment of a Karjat-bound fast local train at Mulund station, killing 11 people and injuring 82.
The attack was preceded by two other explosions. On December 6, 2002, a bomb blast at Mumbai Central railway station injured 27 people, while on January 27, 2003, a woman was killed in a blast at Vile Parle.
The first arrest was made by the Crime Branch in April 2003 when Saquib Nachan was taken into custody. Investigators later alleged that he and Lashkar-e-Taiba member Faisal Khan had masterminded the attack along with 23 others. Of the 25 accused, five, including Khan, later died.
Saquib Nachan, former general secretary of the banned Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI), and Muzammil Ansari, along with eight others, were convicted in the case.
On August 25, 2003, twin blasts at the Gateway of India and Zaveri Bazaar killed 54 people and injured 244 after explosives planted in taxis detonated.
The Mumbai Police arrested Ashrat Ansari, his associate Hanif Sayed Anees and Anees’s wife Fehmida Sayed, along with others. They were charged under various provisions of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (POTA) and the Indian Penal Code.

In 2009, a special POTA court awarded the death penalty to the trio. According to the prosecution, the conspiracy was hatched in Dubai with support from certain Pakistani nationals. The prosecution argued that the attack was intended to avenge the deaths of members of the minority community in the aftermath of the Godhra incident.
On July 11, 2006, seven near-simultaneous bomb blasts struck first-class compartments of suburban trains across Mumbai between 6.23 p.m. and 6.29 p.m. The coordinated explosions killed 187 people and injured about 824 others.
The police claimed to have cracked the case on September 6, 2006, citing call data records that allegedly established links between the accused, Lashkar-e-Taiba and Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence. Investigators alleged that several accused had sheltered Pakistani terrorists and facilitated their entry into India through the India-Nepal and India-Bangladesh borders. Explosives containing RDX and ammonium nitrate were reportedly carried in pressure cookers packed inside bags and placed on trains departing from Churchgate.
The Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) arrested 13 people in connection with the case, several of them linked to the banned SIMI. According to the chargesheet, they were taken to Pakistan for training before returning to India to execute the conspiracy.
Near-simultaneous bomb blasts rocked the busy neighbourhoods of Zaveri Bazaar, Opera House and Dadar during the evening rush hour on July 13, 2011, killing 23 people and injuring 127 others.
The most powerful blast, suspected to have been caused by an improvised explosive device (IED), occurred at Zaveri Bazaar in south Mumbai. The second struck Kabutarkhana near Dadar railway station, while the third occurred at Opera House. The 2011 attack marked the third blast at Zaveri Bazaar, following earlier explosions in 1993 and 2003.
Investigators from the Maharashtra ATS and the Mumbai Crime Branch alleged that ₹10 lakh was routed through hawala channels and delivered to Kawalnayan Wazirchand Pathreja, a hawala operator from Ghaziabad, who allegedly passed the money to Indian Mujahideen operative Yasin Bhatkal, identified as one of the key conspirators. The funds were allegedly distributed among other accused involved in the plot.
The ATS said it had arrested three men linked to the planning and execution of the attacks, one of whom later turned witness. Investigators alleged that Naquee Ahmed Sheikh and Nadeem Akhtar Ashfaq Sheikh, both from Darbhanga in Bihar, stole the scooters used to plant the bombs and transported explosives and detonators from New Delhi. However, police said three key suspects, including Indian Mujahideen commander Muhammad Ahmad Zarar Siddibapa, remained absconding.
